analysis.one_liner: Expands the earned income tax credit and sends families monthly child tax credit payments.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 43 Senate cosponsors — every one a Democrat or independent, including the Finance Committee chair — but never received a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the child tax credit to $250 or $300 per child per month, paid monthly, and make it fully refundable so families with little or no income tax bill still get the full amount. It would also roughly double the earned income tax credit for workers without children and open it to adults as young as 19 (18 for former foster or homeless youth) and past 65. The bill never got a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income families with children would receive $250 per month per qualifying child ($300 for children under 6), fully refundable. Workers without children between 19 and any age would get a much larger earned income credit, phased in at 15.3% of earnings instead of 7.65%, with higher income limits. Parents who lose a job mid-year could count prior-year earnings to keep the credit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low- and middle-income families and childless workers

how_it_helps.text: Sets the child tax credit at $250 per qualifying month per child ($300 for children under 6), paid monthly in advance rather than once a year at tax time, and makes it fully refundable.
Doubles the earned income credit phase-in for childless workers from 7.65% to 15.3% of earnings and raises their income limits from $4,220/$5,280 to $9,820/$11,610.
Lowers the minimum EITC age from 25 to 19 (18 for former foster or homeless youth) and removes the 65 age cap, and extends the EITC and child credit to Puerto Rico and other territories permanently.

Lets taxpayers whose earnings fell during the year elect to use the prior year's income to calculate the credit, and directs the IRS to build a multilingual online portal for updating family information.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. The bill contains no offsetting revenue — no tax increase on any income group or industry — so the expanded credits would be financed entirely by borrowing, borne by future taxpayers generally.

drawbacks.text: The bill has no pay-for: the permanent expansion of two large tax credits would be financed entirely by added federal deficits, a cost an honest supporter must acknowledge.

Monthly advance payments create overpayment risk: the bill's own recapture provisions show families whose income rises mid-year, who move, or who fail to renew eligibility could owe money back at tax time.
Expanding the childless EITC down to age 19 and eliminating the 65 age cap broadens the credit well beyond parents, increasing its long-run cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is large and targeted: direct monthly cash to families with children and a much bigger wage supplement for low-paid childless workers, both proven to cut child and worker poverty. The cost is real but diffuse — permanent deficit-financed spending with no identified payer. The administrative design (monthly payments with presumptive eligibility and recapture) is more complex than an annual credit and creates clawback risk for families with unstable incomes, though the bill includes grace periods and hardship exceptions to soften that.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, never got a markup or vote there, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on June 14, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
43 senators cosponsored — 41 of the 48 Senate Democrats and 2 of the 4 independents, including Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and Finance Chair Ron Wyden.
The action history shows no committee markup, no committee vote, no floor action after the June 2023 referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The tax code stayed exactly as it was. No industry or income group bore any new cost, and higher-income households and the deficit were spared the financing burden — while the low- and middle-income families the bill was written for got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; targeted families gained nothing

industries.note: The fully refundable, monthly child credit is financed by deficit spending with no offset, and the credit phases down at higher incomes — though the bill's two-tier phaseout actually lets very high earners keep more of the base credit than the 2021 version did. The cost falls on the Treasury rather than directly on any industry.
